title: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
summary: How DiskANN serves billions of vectors from an SSD (Vamana, beam search, page layout, filters, updates), how CAGRA builds and searches graphs on GPUs, and how to measure both.
outcomes: Explain why in-memory graph indexes stop scaling and what an SSD-resident index must minimize
Run Vamana's RobustPrune by hand and predict how alpha changes the edges kept
Estimate SSD reads and round trips per query from beam width W, list size L and PQ code size
Compute how page layout changes 4 KB reads per query, and size DiskANN's search RAM budget
Describe how FreshDiskANN applies updates and how Filtered-DiskANN builds label-aware graphs
Trace NN-descent, CAGRA's rank-based pruning and one GPU search iteration
Build, sweep and measure a DiskANN or CAGRA index, and choose between DiskANN, CAGRA and HNSW

lessons.title: Why a billion vectors break in-memory graph indexes

blocks.md: In the prerequisite course you saw HNSW: a proximity graph that greedy search walks toward the query, touching only a tiny fraction of the vectors. HNSW assumes the whole graph and every full-precision vector sit in RAM. That assumption is what breaks first when the dataset grows to a billion points.

Do the arithmetic for $N = 10^9$ vectors of 128 dimensions. Stored as float32 they take $10^9 \times 128 \times 4$ bytes = 512 GB. A graph with $R = 64$ neighbor ids per node, 4 bytes each, adds another 256 GB. Here $R$ is the maximum out-degree: the cap on how many neighbors one node may list. A single workstation with 64 GB of RAM cannot hold either one. The bars below compute these footprints and compare them with 32-byte product-quantization (PQ) codes, which you met in the PQ course.

blocks.title: Memory for one billion 128-d vectors (GB)

scenes.caption: An in-memory graph index needs the full vectors plus the adjacency lists: 512 + 256 = 768 GB for float32 data with 64 neighbors per node.
PQ with 32 bytes per vector shrinks the vectors to 32 GB, which fits in 64 GB of RAM. Everything else has to live somewhere cheaper.
DiskANN's split: only the 32 GB of PQ codes stay in RAM; full vectors and the graph (768 GB) go to an SSD, which costs far less per byte than DRAM.

blocks.md:
Before DiskANN there were two standard ways to cope, and the DiskANN paper (Subramanya et al., NeurIPS 2019) explains why both hurt:

- **Inverted index plus compression** (IVF with PQ, as in FAISS): small enough for one machine, but the lossy codes cap accuracy. The paper reports 1-recall@1 (the fraction of queries whose first result is the true nearest neighbor) around 0.5 for such billion-scale indexes.
- **Sharding in-memory graphs**: high recall, but many machines. The paper cites a deployment splitting 2 billion vectors into 32 shards on 32 machines.

Why not just put the graph on an SSD? A retail SSD needs a few hundred microseconds per random read and serves roughly 300K random reads per second. Greedy search reads one node, waits, then decides the next node. Each such wait is one **round trip**: the search sends its reads to the SSD and can do nothing until they come back, so plain greedy search pays one round trip per node it visits. The paper states the goal precisely: a few dozen random reads per query and fewer than ten round trips to the disk, preferably five. Naively moving an in-memory index to SSD costs several hundred reads per query.

Two numbers drive an SSD-resident index: **total reads per query** (limits throughput, since the SSD has a fixed IOPS budget) and **round trips per query** (limits latency, since each trip costs a few hundred microseconds). DiskANN attacks both: a graph with short search paths, and a search that issues several reads per round trip.

blocks.title: Where DiskANN keeps each piece

scenes.caption: The RAM side holds only compressed PQ codes plus an optional cache of nodes near the start node. The SSD holds one fixed-size record per node.
Search compares the query to PQ codes in RAM to decide which nodes to fetch, then reads those nodes' records (neighbor lists) from the SSD.
Each SSD record also holds the node's full-precision vector, so the final top candidates are re-ranked with exact distances at no extra I/O.

blocks.md: GPUs push in the other direction. They have high memory bandwidth and thousands of threads, but graph search is sequential (each hop depends on the one before) and branchy (what runs next depends on the data, so threads built to run in lockstep end up waiting for each other). **CAGRA** (Ootomo et al., ICDE 2024, from NVIDIA) redesigns both the graph and the search so a GPU can build and search it fast. The plot lets you check footprints yourself for other sizes.

blocks.title: Footprint versus dataset size

scenes.caption: Default: 128-d float32, R = 64, 32-byte PQ. At one billion points the full vectors need 512 GB, the graph 256 GB, the PQ codes 32 GB.
With 96-d vectors and R = 32 the full data still exceeds 64 GB of RAM long before a billion points, while PQ codes stay small.

blocks.question: A team stores a 1-billion-point, 128-d float32 graph index on SSD and searches it with plain greedy search, one node read per step. Queries take 300 node visits. What is the main problem?
options: The SSD runs out of capacity
Hundreds of sequential round trips, each a few hundred microseconds, push latency far beyond a few milliseconds
PQ codes do not fit in RAM
Greedy search cannot run on data stored on disk
blocks.explain: 300 sequential reads at a few hundred microseconds each is tens of milliseconds or more. DiskANN's paper targets a few dozen reads and fewer than ten round trips. Capacity is fine (768 GB fits on SSD), and 32 GB of PQ codes fit in 64 GB of RAM.

blocks.question: Why does DiskANN keep PQ codes for every point in RAM instead of reading vectors from the SSD to compute distances during the search?
options: Each neighbor's distance would then cost its own random read, multiplying I/O by the degree
PQ distances are exact
The SSD cannot store full vectors
RAM is cheaper than SSD
blocks.explain: Search must score every neighbor of every expanded node, which is dozens of distance computations per hop. Fetching each neighbor's vector from SSD would be a random read per neighbor. Approximate PQ distances in RAM steer the search; exact vectors are only needed for the nodes actually read.

lessons.title: Vamana: RobustPrune and the alpha knob

blocks.md: Vamana is the graph DiskANN builds. Like HNSW and NSG (Navigating Spreading-out Graph, Fu et al., VLDB 2019, a single-layer proximity graph) it is made of two routines: **GreedySearch**$(s, x_q, k, L)$, a best-first walk from a start node $s$ toward the query vector $x_q$ that keeps a list of the $L$ closest nodes seen and returns the best $k$, and **RobustPrune**$(p, \mathcal{V}, \alpha, R)$, which picks at most $R$ out-neighbors for node $p$ from a candidate set $\mathcal{V}$. The new ingredient is the parameter $\alpha \ge 1$.

RobustPrune works greedily. Take the candidate $p^*$ closest to $p$ and add the edge $p \to p^*$. Then delete from the candidate set every $p'$ that $p^*$ already covers, meaning a search sitting at $p^*$ is clearly closer to $p'$ than a search sitting at $p$. Repeat until the candidates run out or $p$ has $R$ edges. The covering test, where $d(a, b)$ is the distance between points a and b (Euclidean in this course), is:

blocks.tex: \text{remove } p' \text{ if } \alpha \cdot d(p^*, p') \le d(p, p')
blocks.caption: With alpha = 1 this is the sparse neighborhood graph (SNG) rule, a relative of the relative neighborhood graph (RNG), which HNSW and NSG use implicitly. With alpha above 1 a candidate is removed only if p star is closer to it than p is, by a factor of alpha.

blocks.md: A toy example on a 2D grid. Node **p** sits at (5, 4); six candidates A to F surround it. Coordinates are the grid positions in the figure, and every distance below is Euclidean, computed by script. Distances from p: B 1.41, D 3.00, C 4.47, F 5.00, A 5.10, E 5.39.

blocks.prompt: Run RobustPrune for p with alpha = 1 and no degree limit. B is picked first. Which of A, C, E, F does B cover? Then guess: will raising alpha to 1.2 add or remove edges?
blocks.reveal:
With alpha = 1, B covers A (4.00 vs 5.10), C (3.16 vs 4.47) and E (5.00 vs 5.39). Next D is picked and covers F (3.16 vs 5.00). Result: **p keeps only B and D**.

With alpha = 1.2, E survives: $1.2 \times 5.00 = 6.00 > 5.39$. B is closer to E than p is, but not by a factor of 1.2. Result: **B, D, E**. Larger alpha keeps *more* edges, and the extra ones are long-range.

blocks.title: RobustPrune for p: alpha = 1 versus 1.2

scenes.caption: Candidates for p with their distance to p. RobustPrune always takes the closest remaining candidate first, so B (1.41) goes first.
alpha = 1: B covers A, C and E because B is closer to each of them than p is (4.00 < 5.10, 3.16 < 4.47, 5.00 < 5.39). Their edges are dropped.
Next D (3.00) is kept and covers F (3.16 < 5.00). With alpha = 1, p ends with just two out-edges: B and D.
alpha = 1.2: B still covers A (4.80 ≤ 5.10) and C (3.79 ≤ 4.47), but not E: 1.2 x 5.00 = 6.00 is more than 5.39. D covers F (3.79 ≤ 5.00).
alpha = 1.5 keeps four edges (B, D, C, E): only F (via D) and A (via C) are covered. Higher alpha gives a denser graph with more long jumps.

blocks.md: Why keep the long edge to E? Under the alpha rule, every edge that survives guarantees real progress. The paper shows that if every node is pruned with RobustPrune over all other points and $\alpha > 1$, greedy search from any start converges to any base point in a logarithmic number of steps. The one-line reason: when $p$ is pruned against all other points with no degree cap, any target $x$ that is not an out-neighbor of $p$ was removed by some kept neighbor $p^*$ with $\alpha \cdot d(p^*, x) \le d(p, x)$. So one hop to $p^*$ divides the remaining distance to $x$ by at least $\alpha$, and repeated hops shrink it geometrically. With $\alpha = 1$ a hop only promises *some* progress, and points on a line give a line graph whose diameter grows like $n$.

blocks.caption: RobustPrune (Algorithm 2 of the DiskANN paper). p_star itself is removed by the filter since its distance to itself is 0.

blocks.md:
**Vamana construction** (Algorithm 3):

1. Start from a random graph where every node has $R$ random out-neighbors. Use the dataset's **medoid** $s$ as the search start: the data point whose total distance to all other points is smallest, a real point at the center of the data, so every search starts near the middle.
2. Visit points in random order. For point $p$, run GreedySearch$(s, x_p, 1, L)$ and collect **every node visited**, not just the final $L$ results.
3. Set $p$'s out-edges with RobustPrune on that visited set.
4. Add the reverse edge $p' \to p$ for each new out-neighbor $p'$. If $p'$ now exceeds $R$ edges, RobustPrune $p'$.

Vamana makes **two passes**: first with $\alpha = 1$, then with the user's $\alpha$ (the paper used $\alpha = 2$ in its experiments). The paper reports that the second pass improves the graph, and that running both passes with large $\alpha$ is slower because the first pass then builds a denser graph. Using the visited set as candidates lets Vamana add long-range edges, which is why it does not need HNSW's layer hierarchy.

A common misreading: larger alpha prunes *more*. It is the opposite. The removal test gets harder to pass as alpha grows, so more candidates survive, the average degree rises (up to the cap R), and search paths get shorter. The cost is memory and more distance computations per hop.

blocks.question: In the toy example, alpha = 1.2 kept the edge p to E even though B is closer to E than p is. Which statement explains why that edge is useful?
options: E is p's nearest neighbor
Going through B would bring a search only slightly closer to E (5.00 vs 5.39), so a direct edge gives much faster progress toward points near E
Vamana keeps every edge longer than 5
alpha only affects the build pass, not which edges exist
blocks.explain: Under alpha = 1.2 an edge is dropped only if the detour node is closer to the target by a factor of 1.2 (for E: within 5.39 / 1.2 = 4.49). B is at 5.00, only about 7 percent closer, so the hop through B makes little progress. Keeping long edges where detours are weak is what shrinks the number of hops.

blocks.question: HNSW passes only the final L search results to its pruning step, while Vamana passes every node visited during the search. What does that change?
options: Vamana's graph has no reverse edges
Nothing, the two sets are identical
Vamana sees far-away nodes from early in the path as candidates, so it can create long-range edges without a hierarchy
HNSW becomes slower to build
blocks.explain: Nodes visited early in a greedy walk are far from p. Giving RobustPrune those candidates (together with alpha above 1) lets p keep some long jumps. HNSW gets long jumps from its upper layers instead, which DiskANN avoids because each layer would mean more disk reads.

lessons.title: DiskANN search: beam width, SSD reads and re-ranking

blocks.md: On disk, DiskANN stores one fixed-size record per node: the node's full-precision vector followed by the ids of its at most $R$ neighbors, padded with zeros if it has fewer. Because every record has the same size, the offset of node $i$ is a multiplication, so no offset table is needed in RAM.

Record size is small. For 128-d float32 vectors and $R = 64$: $128 \times 4 + 64 \times 4 = 768$ bytes. The paper notes that reading a 4 KB-aligned block (4 KB starting at a multiple of 4 KB, the unit an SSD reads in) costs no more than reading 512 bytes, so a node's neighbor list and its full vector arrive in one read.

**BeamSearch** changes one thing in GreedySearch. Instead of expanding the single closest unexpanded candidate, it takes the $W$ closest unexpanded candidates from the list $\mathcal{L}$, fetches all $W$ records in one parallel batch, and scores their neighbors with PQ distances. The paper notes that a few random reads in parallel cost almost the same time as one. $W = 1$ is plain greedy search.

blocks.prompt: Beam width W = 4 instead of W = 1, same list size L = 40. Guess what happens to (a) total SSD reads per query and (b) round trips.
blocks.reveal: Round trips drop sharply (about 3.3x), but total reads go **up** a little, because some of the W nodes fetched in a batch would never have been expanded by a one-at-a-time search. In the simulation below: W = 1 needs 41.5 reads in 41.5 trips, W = 4 needs 44.4 reads in 12.5 trips.

blocks.title: Beam width versus SSD reads (toy simulation, L = 40)

scenes.caption: Average reads (node records fetched) per query. They creep up with W: wider beams fetch some nodes a narrow search would skip.
Average round trips per query. Each trip fetches up to W records in parallel, so trips fall roughly as 1/W.
Recall@10 barely moves (in percent). Beam width is a latency knob, not an accuracy knob; L controls accuracy.

blocks.md: The simulation behind those bars: 5,000 random 32-d Gaussian vectors, Vamana built with $R = 32$, $L = 64$ and passes at $\alpha = 1$ then $1.2$, searched with exact distances from the medoid for 200 queries. Simplified: real DiskANN steers with PQ distances and caches nodes near the start, which removes the first few reads.

blocks.title: Search latency if each round trip costs 200 microseconds

scenes.caption: Model: latency = round trips x 200 us (a stated assumption; the paper says a few hundred microseconds per trip). W = 1 takes 41.5 trips, about 8.3 ms.
W = 2 halves the trips: 22.0 trips, 4.4 ms.
W = 4 and W = 8: 2.5 ms and 1.6 ms. Returns diminish: going from 4 to 8 saves under 1 ms but adds 5 reads per query to the SSD's budget.

blocks.md: The paper explains why you should not just max out W. An SSD reaches its peak IOPS only with deep queues (many reads outstanding at once, so its internal flash chips all work in parallel), and then each read takes over a millisecond. DiskANN runs at beam widths like 2, 4 or 8, where the SSD sits at a 30 to 40 percent load and each search thread spends 40 to 50 percent of its time in I/O. It also warns that W of 16 or more wastes compute and bandwidth. The legacy repository's docs say the same: use W = 1 for the highest throughput at a fixed IOPS rating, W = 4 or 8 for best latency (default 2).

blocks.title: Real DiskANN run from the repository docs (W = 2, 100K SIFT)

scenes.caption: Mean 4 KB reads per query grow almost linearly with the search list size L: 8.8 reads at L = 10, 76.6 at L = 100.
Recall@10 in percent for the same runs. Going from L = 20 to L = 100 buys 3.5 points of recall for almost 5x the reads.

blocks.md:
Two more tricks finish the design:

- **Caching**: keep in DRAM the records of all nodes within C = 3 or 4 hops of the start node (or nodes chosen from a known query distribution). The first hops of every query then cost no I/O.
- **Implicit re-ranking**: PQ distances are approximate, so the final order can be wrong. Every record read during search already carries the full vector, so DiskANN re-ranks the visited nodes with exact distances using no extra reads.

**What PQ error does to the walk.** The simulation above steered with exact distances. Real DiskANN steers with PQ codes, so the list $\mathcal{L}$ is ordered by approximate distances. To see the effect we wrote a small simulator (our code, not DiskANN's): a Vamana graph on SIFT10K (the 10,000-vector SIFT benchmark used in the HNSW course) built with $R = 32$, $L = 50$ and $\alpha = 1.2$, the settings of the repository's example, then beam search with $W = 4$ and $L = 40$, steered by exact distances or by 32-, 16- or 8-byte PQ codes trained on the SIFT learning set. An exhaustive scan with these codes gives the same recall@10 as in the HNSW course: 84.1, 72.1 and 58.8 percent.

blocks.prompt: Same graph, same L = 40 and W = 4. Switch the steering from 32-byte to 8-byte PQ codes. Guess what happens to (a) SSD reads per query and (b) recall@10 after the free re-rank with full vectors.
blocks.reveal:
(a) Reads barely move: 50.0 with 32-byte codes, 50.5 with 8-byte codes. At a fixed L the walk expands about L + 10 nodes whatever steers it.

(b) Recall after re-ranking falls from 99.8 to 90.2 percent. Coarse codes misorder the list, so the walk spends its reads on nodes that are not the true neighbors, and a neighbor that is never read can never be re-ranked.

blocks.title: Steering with PQ codes on SIFT10K (our simulator, L = 40, W = 4)

scenes.caption: Reads (node records fetched) per query, averaged over the 100 SIFT10K queries: 49.8, 50.0, 49.5, 50.5. The code size does not change how many nodes a fixed L expands.
Recall@10 of the list itself, before re-ranking: 99.9, 84.0, 72.2, 58.5 percent. The list is only as good as the codes that ordered it, nearly the exhaustive PQ scan's 84.1, 72.1 and 58.8.
Recall@10 after re-ranking the expanded nodes with the full vectors their records carry: 99.9, 99.8, 99.2, 90.2. Re-ranking repairs the order, but not the neighbors the 8-byte walk never read.

blocks.md: So where do more PQ bytes pay? In the reads needed for a recall target. In the same simulator, 8-byte codes needed $L = 100$ (109 reads) to reach 97.7 percent recall@10 and $L = 200$ (207.7 reads) to reach 99.7. 32-byte codes reached 97.8 percent at $L = 20$ (31.4 reads) and 99.8 at $L = 40$ (50.0 reads): about 3.5 to 4 times fewer reads for the same recall. This is why the repository ties the RAM budget to the PQ code size: more bytes per point in RAM buy fewer SSD reads per query at the same recall.

For billion-point builds the paper avoids needing 1.1 TB of RAM: k-means splits the data into 40 clusters, each point joins its 2 closest clusters, a Vamana index is built per cluster in memory, and the graphs are merged by taking the union of edges. On SIFT1B (one billion 128-d SIFT descriptors, the billion-point version of the SIFT1M benchmark from the PQ course) this produced a 348 GB index with average degree 92.1, built within 64 GB of RAM. Searched on a 16-core workstation, DiskANN served over 5,000 queries per second at under 3 ms mean latency with 95 percent plus 1-recall@1.

Why must each point join **two** clusters? A point assigned to two clusters appears in two per-cluster graphs, so after the union its edges lead into both. These shared points are the bridges between the pieces. With one cluster per point the union would be 40 disconnected graphs, and a search that starts in one cluster could never reach a neighbor filed in another. The repository exposes this path through `-M` (build_DRAM_budget): when the budget is too small for a one-shot build, the code partitions the data with each point in its 2 closest partitions, builds each piece, and overlays them, which the docs say can be up to 1.5x slower.

Beam width W trades round trips for wasted reads; search list L trades reads for recall. Tune L for the recall target first, then pick the smallest W that meets the latency target, watching total reads against the SSD's IOPS budget.

blocks.question: A DiskANN service is limited by SSD IOPS at peak traffic, and p99 latency is comfortably under target. Which change is most sensible?
options: Increase W from 4 to 16
Increase L to raise recall
Lower W toward 1 to cut total reads per query
Turn off re-ranking
blocks.explain: Smaller beams waste fewer reads, so each query consumes less of the IOPS budget; latency rises but there is headroom. The repository docs recommend W = 1 for the highest throughput at a fixed IOPS rating. Re-ranking costs no extra reads, so disabling it saves nothing.

blocks.question: Why does DiskANN's re-ranking with full-precision vectors cost no extra SSD reads?
options: Full vectors are cached in RAM
Each node's full vector is stored in the same disk block as its neighbor list, so it arrives with the read the search already made
Re-ranking uses PQ codes only
It reads all candidates in one big sequential read
blocks.explain: The record layout puts the vector next to the adjacency list, inside one 4 KB read. Re-ranking piggybacks on reads the beam search needed anyway. The paper contrasts this with an earlier system that fetched about a hundred candidate vectors at the end, in one burst of random reads.

lessons.title: Beyond beam search: SSD page layout and I/O efficiency

blocks.md: Lesson 3 left one waste untouched. A node record is small, 768 bytes for 128-d float32 with $R = 64$, but the SSD reads 4 KB at a time. In the DiskANN code a record is the vector, a neighbor count and $R$ ids, $(R + 1) \times 4 + D \times \text{sizeof}(T)$ bytes, which is 772 bytes here, and records are packed $\lfloor 4096 / 772 \rfloor = 5$ to a 4 KB sector **in id order**: nodes 0 to 4 share one sector, 5 to 9 the next. Every read therefore brings in five records, and the search uses one.

blocks.caption: For 128-d float32 and R = 64. For the SIFT10K graph used below (R = 32), a record is 644 bytes, 6 fit in a sector, and one useful record is 15.7 percent of the read.

blocks.md: Why can't the other four records help? Ids follow input order, which has nothing to do with the graph. At a billion points the four nodes sharing a sector with the one you want are effectively random, so the chance one of them is useful to this query is near zero. **Starling** (Wang et al., SIGMOD 2024) measured DiskANN on BIGANN: I/O took up to 92.5 percent of search time, and up to 94 percent of the vertices in each loaded block were wasted. Its fix keeps the graph and changes where the nodes sit, so that a node and its neighbors share a block.

blocks.title: One 9-hop search on a 24-node toy graph, 4 nodes per page

scenes.caption: The search visits nodes 18, 13, 9, 5, 3, 17, 16, 10, 21 (graph and path computed by script). In id order those 9 nodes fall in all 6 pages: 6 reads even if a page, once read, were kept for the rest of the query.
DiskANN does not even keep pages: it issues one read per expanded node, 9 reads for 9 hops, each 4 KB for one useful record.
Reordered with BNP (each node followed by its unplaced neighbors), the same 9 nodes sit in pages 0, 1, 4 and 5: 4 reads, and pages 2 and 3 are never touched.

blocks.md:
Starling defines the goal precisely. For a node $u$, its **overlap ratio** $OR(u)$ is the fraction of the other nodes in $u$'s block that are $u$'s neighbors; $OR(G)$ averages it over all nodes. **Block shuffling** reassigns nodes to blocks to maximize $OR(G)$. The paper proves this is NP-hard, then gives three heuristics:

- **BNP** (block neighbor padding): scan ids in order; put each unplaced node and its unplaced neighbors into the current block.
- **BNF** (block neighbor frequency): starting from BNP, repeatedly move each node to the block holding most of its neighbors. The paper recommends it, at 3 to 10 percent of graph build time.
- **BNS** (block neighbor swap): swap nodes between blocks when that raises the overlap; slowest, best $OR(G)$.

Two search changes use the new layout. **Block search**: when a block arrives, compute exact distances for every node in it (the vectors are right there), add them to the results, and also scan the neighbor lists of the closest ones for new candidates (the paper keeps the top 30 percent), so one read does the work of several hops. Our simulator below uses a simpler variant: it adds the block's nodes as candidates, so later hops to them cost no read. **In-memory navigation graph**: a small graph over a sample of the vectors, kept in RAM, picks an entry point near the query, so the disk walk skips the long approach from a fixed start node. The first change raises useful records per read; the second shortens the path.

blocks.prompt: Reordering cuts the pages a query reads. Will it also cut round trips (latency) as much? Think about what decides the number of round trips in beam search.
blocks.reveal: Mostly not. Round trips are set by how many beam steps the walk takes, and reordering does not change the graph, so the walk is nearly the same length. In the measurement below, BNF plus block search cut reads from 50.0 to 36.2 per query but round trips only from 13.5 to 13.1. Shortening the path itself, with entry points from an in-memory graph, is what cut round trips, to 11.4. Fewer reads mainly help throughput under a fixed IOPS budget.

blocks.md: We measured the effect with the same simulator and SIFT10K graph as lesson 3 (32-byte PQ steering, $W = 4$, $L = 40$, 644-byte records, 6 per sector). For the layouts, a page read earlier in the query is not read again, and BNP and a simplified BNF are our implementations of the paper's descriptions. The overlap ratio was 0.007 in id order, 0.177 after BNP and 0.224 after three BNF passes. Navigation entry points come from a 100-point sample searched in RAM, a stand-in for Starling's navigation graph. At this toy scale even id order sometimes shares a page; at a billion points it would not.

blocks.title: Page layout and block search on SIFT10K (our simulator, L = 40, W = 4)

scenes.caption: 4 KB reads per query: 50.0 when every expanded node costs a read, 48.7 in id order with page reuse, 41.3 after BNP, 37.5 after BNF, 36.2 with block search, 30.1 with entry points chosen in RAM.
Round trips per query: 13.5, 13.5, 13.3, 13.2, 13.1, 11.4. Layout barely moves them; a closer entry point does.
Recall@10 in percent stays at 99.8 to 99.9 throughout: reordering moves bytes, not answers.

blocks.md: On an SSD the cost unit is the 4 KB page, not the node. Count pages read and useful records per page. A layout that co-locates graph neighbors raises records per page; an entry point near the query shortens the path. Neither changes the graph or the recall.

Starling targets vector databases that split data into **segments** (see *Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk*), where each segment gets a small slice of the machine. The paper's segment has under 2 GB of memory and 10 GB of disk; there Starling held 33 million 128-d vectors at over 0.9 recall@10 with latency under 1 ms, and reports 43.9x higher throughput with 98 percent lower latency than state-of-the-art methods at the same accuracy.

Whatever the layout, size the RAM first. The repository gives the search RAM budget `-B` as the PQ codes plus a cache of about 250,000 nodes:

blocks.caption: n points, b PQ bytes per point, max degree R, D dimensions of type T. For 100M 128-d float32 points, b = 32, R = 64: 2.98 + 0.18 = 3.16 GB. This is the docs' formula; the code reserves 0.25 GB of any B above 1.25 GB for the cache, so 3.16 gives 31-byte codes.

blocks.question: One billion 96-d float32 points, 32-byte PQ codes, R = 64. Using the repository's formula, what search RAM budget B should you pass?
options: About 3.2 GB
About 384 GB, the size of the full vectors
About 30 GB: 29.80 for the PQ codes plus 0.15 for the 250,000-node cache
About 0.15 GB, since only the cache lives in RAM
blocks.explain: n b / 2^30 = 10^9 x 32 / 2^30 = 29.80 GB for the codes. The cache term is 250,000 x (4 x 64 + 4 x 96) / 2^30 = 0.15 GB. Full vectors stay on the SSD; about 3.1 GB (2.98 + 0.15) would be the answer for 100M such points.

blocks.question: A DiskANN deployment is limited by SSD IOPS and its p99 latency is fine. Which change attacks the bottleneck most directly without touching recall?
options: Raise the beam width W from 4 to 8
Raise L
Lower alpha to 1 to make the graph sparser
Reorder the on-disk layout so graph neighbors share 4 KB pages, and score every record in each page read
blocks.explain: IOPS-bound means reads per query are the cost. Co-locating neighbors plus block search cut reads per query (50.0 to 36.2 in our run) at the same recall. A wider beam adds reads, a larger L adds reads, and a sparser graph lengthens paths.

lessons.title: FreshDiskANN: inserts and deletes without rebuilds

blocks.md: A static index is rebuilt from scratch when data changes. The FreshDiskANN paper (Singh et al., 2021) notes that building a good HNSW index over 100M points takes about 1.5 to 2 hours on a 48-core machine, so keeping a billion-point index six-hourly fresh would need three machines doing nothing but rebuilds. Real systems need inserts and deletes while queries keep running.

Inserts are easy: run GreedySearch for the new point, RobustPrune the visited set to get its out-edges, and add reverse edges (re-pruning any node that exceeds $R$). Deletes are the hard part. The paper tested two natural policies on HNSW, NSG and Vamana, deleting and re-inserting 5 percent of SIFT1M per cycle:

- **Policy A**: drop the deleted node's edges.
- **Policy B**: also connect each in-neighbor to each of the deleted node's out-neighbors, then prune.

Recall kept falling cycle after cycle for all three graphs.

Their diagnosis: aggressive pruning ($\alpha = 1$) makes the graph sparser with every update, so it becomes less navigable. **FreshVamana** applies Policy B with RobustPrune at $\alpha > 1$ (Algorithm 4), which keeps the graph dense. Their experiments show stable recall over 50 cycles of updates, except when $\alpha = 1$.

Toy example on the lesson 2 points. Each node's out-edges come from RobustPrune over all other points with $\alpha = 1.2$ and $R = 3$ (computed by script). Node p has edges to B, D, E, and B has edges to p, C, F. Now B is deleted.

blocks.title: Consolidating a delete around node p

scenes.caption: Before: p points to B, D, E. B points to C and F (and back to p). B is about to be deleted.
Lazy delete: B goes on the DeleteList. Searches may still route through B but never return it. The graph is not touched yet.
Consolidation for p: candidates = p's surviving neighbors {D, E} plus B's neighbors {C, F}. Distances to p: D 3.00, C 4.47, F 5.00, E 5.39.
RobustPrune(alpha 1.2): keep D, which covers F (3.79 ≤ 5.00); keep C, which covers E (1.2 x 4.12 = 4.95 ≤ 5.39). p's new edges: D and C. The path p, B, C became p, C.

blocks.md: Deleting eagerly would mean editing every in-neighbor of every deleted node immediately. FreshVamana is lazy: a delete just adds the id to a **DeleteList**. After a non-trivial batch accumulates (the paper suggests 1 to 10 percent of the index), a parallel **delete consolidation** pass runs Algorithm 4 for all affected nodes at once.

The full **FreshDiskANN** system has three parts:

- **LTI** (long-term index): the SSD-resident DiskANN index, with about 25 to 32 bytes of PQ data per point in RAM. Updates do not touch it in real time.
- **TempIndex**: in-memory FreshVamana indexes holding recent inserts. One read-write instance takes inserts; it is periodically frozen into a read-only instance and snapshotted to disk.
- **DeleteList**: ids deleted but still present in some index.

blocks.title: FreshDiskANN request flow

scenes.caption: An insert goes only to the read-write TempIndex in RAM, which runs the FreshVamana insert.
A delete just appends the id to the DeleteList.
A search queries the LTI and every TempIndex, merges results, and filters out ids on the DeleteList.
When the read-only TempIndexes exceed a memory threshold, StreamingMerge folds inserts and deletes into the LTI in the background.

blocks.md:
**StreamingMerge** must use memory proportional to the change, not the index, and keep serving queries. It runs three phases:

1. **Delete**: stream the LTI block by block, run Algorithm 4 on each block, write it back.
2. **Insert**: for each new point, GreedySearch the SSD index and RobustPrune its candidates. Backward edges are not written yet; they go into an in-memory structure $\Delta$.
3. **Patch**: stream the index again, add the $\Delta$ edges to each node, prune if over $R$, write back.

All distance comparisons use the in-memory PQ codes, which is why recall settles slightly below a fresh static build.

The paper gives concrete costs: exactly two sequential passes over the SSD data, about 100 random 4 KB reads per inserted point (a candidate list of 75), and $\Delta$ of size $O(|N| R)$, where $|N|$ is the number of inserted points, because each new point adds at most $R$ backward edges. For 30M inserts at $R = 64$ that is at most 1.92 billion edge entries; at 4 bytes per id, about 7.7 billion bytes, in line with the paper's estimate of about 7 GB. Note the newer DiskANN3 library in the same repository describes real-time updates with stable recall using logic from FreshDiskANN and IP-DiskANN (in-place DiskANN, Xu et al., 2025, which applies each insert and delete directly to the graph instead of batching deletes for a consolidation pass), without merges.

Do not drop a deleted node's edges and move on. That was Policy A, and recall decayed over update cycles for every graph tested. Repair the neighborhood (connect in-neighbors to the deleted node's out-neighbors) and prune with alpha above 1.

blocks.question: In the toy consolidation, why do B's out-neighbors C and F become candidates for p?
options: Because they are p's nearest points
Because RobustPrune always adds every candidate
Because paths that ran p, B, C or p, B, F must be preserved by giving p a chance to link to them directly
Because C and F were on the DeleteList
blocks.explain: Algorithm 4 adds the deleted node's out-neighbors to the candidate set of each in-neighbor, so navigation through the hole is preserved. RobustPrune then decides which to keep: here C survives and F is covered by D.

blocks.question: A FreshDiskANN deployment sees recall slowly drift down over weeks of merges. The build used alpha = 1 to keep the index small. What is the likely fix?
options: Rebuild with alpha above 1 so update rules keep the graph dense
Increase the DeleteList size
Merge more often
Turn off PQ
blocks.explain: The FreshDiskANN experiments show recall stays stable across update cycles for alpha above 1 but not for alpha = 1, because repeated alpha = 1 pruning makes the graph progressively sparser.

blocks.md: Real queries carry conditions: the nearest ads that may run in region X, the nearest documents in tenant Y. **Filtered-DiskANN** (Gollapudi et al., WWW 2023) gives every point a set of **labels** and every query a label; a valid result shares at least one label with the query. Why the obvious fixes fail is covered in *Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata*: post-filtering returns too few results for rare labels, and a plain graph restricted to matching nodes falls apart. The general trade-offs, and predicate-agnostic indexes, belong to that course and to *Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal*. This lesson is DiskANN's own answer: build the labels into the graph.

Back to the lesson 2 toy, now with labels: p, A, C and F are **red**; B, D and E are **blue**. Plain RobustPrune with $\alpha = 1.2$ gave p the out-edges B, D and E. All three are blue. A red query whose search may only step on red nodes starts at p and has nowhere to go: within the red subgraph, p has no out-edges at all.

blocks.tex: \text{remove } p' \text{ only if } \alpha \cdot d(p^*, p') \le d(p, p') \ \text{ and } \ F_p \cap F_{p'} \subseteq F_{p^*}
blocks.caption: FilteredRobustPrune (Algorithm 3). F_x is the label set of x. A kept neighbor p star may cover p' only if p star carries every label that p and p' share, so a search for any of those labels can still go through p star.

blocks.prompt: Run filter-aware RobustPrune for p (alpha = 1.2, no degree cap). B goes first. Can blue B cover red A and red C, as it did before? Which edges does p keep?
blocks.reveal: No. p and A share {red}, and B's labels {blue} do not contain red, so B may not cover A or C; for the same reason D may not cover F. Next in distance order is D, then C (red), which covers A ($1.2 \times 1.41 = 1.70 \le 5.10$) and also E ($1.2 \times 4.12 = 4.95 \le 5.39$; p and E share no label, and the empty set is inside any label set). Result: **B, D, C, F**. With $R = 3$ the closest three stay: B, D, C.

blocks.title: Plain versus filter-aware RobustPrune for p (alpha = 1.2)

scenes.caption: Plain RobustPrune: B covers A and C, D covers F. p keeps B, D, E, all blue, so a red-only walk from p is stuck.
Filter-aware: B and D lack the label red that p shares with A, C and F, so they may not cover them. All three red candidates survive their pass.
Red C is kept next and covers A (1.70 below 5.10) and E (4.95 below 5.39). p ends with B, D, C, F; with R = 3, B, D and C. p now has a red out-neighbor.

blocks.md: **FilteredGreedySearch** (Algorithm 1) starts from the start node of each query label and adds to its list only out-neighbors that share a query label. On the toy we built full graphs over the 7 points ($R = 3$, by script) and searched for a red query at (0.5, 5.5) from p. Plain graph: the search visits only p and returns p, 4.74 away. Filter-aware graph: it visits p, C, A and returns A and C, each 0.71 away.

**FilteredVamana** (Algorithm 4) builds incrementally from an empty graph. For each point $x$: run FilteredGreedySearch from the start nodes of $x$'s labels, prune the visited set with FilteredRobustPrune to get $x$'s out-edges, add the reverse edges, and re-prune any node that exceeds $R$.

Start nodes come from **FindMedoid**, which despite its name is a load balancer: for each label it samples $\tau$ points carrying that label and picks the one already serving as a start node for the fewest labels. If one point started many labels, its $R$ edges could not lead into all of them.

**StitchedVamana** (Algorithm 5) needs all labels up front. It builds an ordinary Vamana graph per label over just the points with that label, with small parameters (the paper used $R_{small} = 32$, $L_{small} = 100$), takes the union of all edges, and runs FilteredRobustPrune on every node down to $R_{stitched} = 64$ with $\alpha = 1.2$. Each node gathers good candidates from every label graph before pruning, which is why it searches faster, but it builds slower and is hard to update: an insert could break the per-label structure. FilteredVamana's label rule is local to one node's neighbors, so inserts fit naturally.

blocks.title: Build time in seconds (Filtered-DiskANN paper, Table 2)

scenes.caption: DANN (3.3M ad embeddings, 47 region labels): 159.8, 469.9 and 158.6 s. StitchedVamana pays about 3x the build time of FilteredVamana.
Prep (1M points): 66.6, 222.6 and 44.5 s. In return, StitchedVamana gave about 2x the QPS of FilteredVamana at 90 percent recall on both datasets.
Turing (2.6M points, labels from enterprise sites): 103.4, 295.9 and 188.0 s. Both graphs kept 90 percent plus recall for labels with specificity from 0.1 down to one in a million.

blocks.md: The paper's other results: on Prep and DANN at 90 percent recall, FilteredVamana ran 2.5x and 3x faster than the best prior method (IVF inline processing), StitchedVamana 6x and 7.5x. On unfiltered queries both still reached 95 percent recall@10, at about 0.8x (Filtered) and 0.9x (Stitched) the QPS of plain Vamana. In an A/B test on sponsored search over 47 regions, FilteredVamana raised clicks by 34.6 percent and revenue by 49.0 percent over the post-filtering production system.

**On the SSD.** Placing these graphs in DiskANN's SSD layout gives Filtered-DiskANN; the paper shows it on 28 million DANN points with $W = 4$. The repository's `build_disk_index` takes the labels as flags:

- `--label_file`: a text file whose line $i$ lists point $i$'s labels, comma-separated.
- `--universal_label`: a label that matches every query; a point carrying it must carry only it.
- `--FilteredLbuild`: the search list size for the filtered build (plain `-L` is for unfiltered builds).
- `--filter_threshold` (`-F`): split nodes with more than F labels; 0, the default, splits nothing.

`search_disk_index` then takes `--filter_label`, and `compute_groundtruth` takes the same label files so recall is measured against the true filtered neighbors.

blocks.md: Filtered-DiskANN serves **label equality** filters known at build time, up to thousands of labels with tens or hundreds per point. The paper handles OR of labels by searching each and merging, and leaves AND as future work. Range, regex or ad-hoc predicates need a predicate-agnostic method; see *Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal*.

blocks.question: Point p has labels {red}, candidate p' has {red, green}, and the kept neighbor p* has {green}. p* is much closer to p' than p is. Does filter-aware RobustPrune remove the edge p to p'?
options: Yes, the distance test passes and p* shares a label with p'
No: p and p' share red, p* lacks red, so a red search could not reach p' through p*
Yes, because p' has more labels than p
No, because filter-aware pruning never removes edges
blocks.explain: The rule needs F_p intersect F_p' = {red} to be inside F_p* = {green}. It is not, so the edge stays. Sharing some label with p' is not enough; p* must carry the labels that p and p' have in common, because those are the searches that would route through it.

blocks.question: A marketplace adds thousands of new listings an hour, each tagged with 1 to 5 of about 800 category labels, and queries filter by one category. Which Filtered-DiskANN build fits?
options: StitchedVamana, rebuilt nightly
A separate Vamana index per category
Plain Vamana with post-filtering
FilteredVamana, which builds incrementally and applies its label rule locally, so new points can be inserted
blocks.explain: The paper notes FilteredVamana suits dynamic growth because its label rule only involves a node's own neighbors. StitchedVamana searches faster but is built from per-label graphs at once, and inserts risk breaking that structure. Per-label indexes multiply storage when points carry several labels; post-filtering fails for rare categories.

lessons.title: CAGRA: a fixed-degree graph built for GPUs

blocks.md: CAGRA (CUDA ANNS GRAph-based; CUDA is NVIDIA's GPU programming platform and ANNS means approximate nearest neighbor search) starts from a different question: what graph shape lets a GPU work efficiently? On an NVIDIA GPU, 32 threads form a **warp** that executes one instruction at a time, warps group into a **cooperative thread array (CTA)**, also called a thread block, that runs on one streaming multiprocessor (SM), one of the GPU's many independent processors, and each CTA has small, fast **shared memory**. Irregular work per node wastes threads.

So the CAGRA graph has three deliberate properties:

- **Fixed out-degree $d$**: every node has exactly $d$ neighbors (this $d$ is the degree, not the distance $d$ of lesson 2). Uniform work per node avoids load imbalance; on a GPU a small degree would leave threads idle anyway.
- **Directed**, as a consequence of fixed out-degree: if X keeps Y, Y's $d$ slots may already be full of closer points, so the edge back from Y to X may not exist.
- **No hierarchy**: instead of HNSW's upper layers, search starts from randomly sampled nodes, which a GPU can score in parallel cheaply.

Construction has two stages. First build a k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) graph, where each node points to its $k$ nearest points, with $k = d_{init}$, typically $2d$ or $3d$. It is built with **NN-descent**, which refines approximate neighbor lists by checking neighbors of neighbors, and each node's list is then sorted by distance. cuVS, NVIDIA's open-source GPU vector search library that implements CAGRA, can also build it with IVF-PQ (the inverted file with PQ codes from the prerequisite courses), and calls $d_{init}$ `intermediate_graph_degree` and $d$ `graph_degree`. A pure kNN graph searches poorly (the paper shows low recall) because neighbor lists are redundant and the graph can split into disconnected pieces. Second, **optimize**: reorder and prune edges, then add reverse edges. The optimization never computes a distance.

**How NN-descent builds the kNN graph.** NN-descent (Dong, Charikar and Li, WWW 2011) rests on one principle: *a neighbor of my neighbor is likely my neighbor*. Start every node with $K$ random neighbors. In each round, every node $v$ looks at its current neighbors and its reverse neighbors (the nodes that list $v$), and compares itself with *their* neighbors; any closer point replaces the farthest entry in $v$'s list. Each round shrinks the radius of the lists, and the algorithm stops when a round changes nothing. The paper reports above 90 percent recall with each point compared against only a few percent of the dataset on average.

blocks.title: One NN-descent update for node K (3-NN lists, 12-point toy)

scenes.caption: Random start on the 12 grid points listed later in this lesson (seed 0, by script): K at (1, 6) holds D, G and F. F is 6.08 away, a poor neighbor. B and C hold K in their own random lists, so they are K's reverse neighbors.
Round 1: K compares itself with the neighborhoods of D, G, F, B and C. C turns up in G's (C lists G) and is only 1.00 from K, so C enters and the farthest entry, F, leaves.
K's list is now C, D, G: exactly its true 3 nearest neighbors. No later round changes it.

blocks.title: NN-descent on the 12-point toy (3-NN lists)

scenes.caption: List updates per round: 45, then 1, then 0, when the algorithm stops. The basic algorithm stops at zero; the paper's practical version stops once a round makes fewer than 0.001 KN updates.

Recall of the lists against the exact 3-NN graph, in percent: 27.8 at random start, 97.2 after one round, 100 after two. With only 12 points, neighbors of neighbors already reach almost everyone; on real data each round sees a small slice.

blocks.md: cuVS offers several builders for this first stage (`build_algo` in Python: `ivf_pq`, the Python default, `nn_descent`, `iterative_cagra_search` and `ace`), and its guide lists their memory: NN-descent copies the dataset to the GPU as fp16 and needs about $N(2D + 276)$ bytes of device memory plus about $N(13I + 912)$ bytes of host memory, where $I$ is `intermediate_graph_degree`. IVF-PQ instead queries an IVF-PQ index in batches, which lets CAGRA build on datasets larger than GPU memory; ACE partitions the data for the same reason. The iterative builder searches the partial CAGRA graph and needs the whole dataset in GPU memory.

**Rank-based reordering.** For an edge X to Y at rank $k$ in X's sorted list, count its **detours**: how many of X's $k$ closer neighbors Z have Y in their own list. Many detours mean Y is easy to reach through other neighbors, so the direct edge is redundant. Keep the $d$ edges with the fewest detours, breaking ties by original rank. This approximates distance by rank, so no distance table is needed.

The toy example below uses 12 grid points: A (1, 0), B (3, 3), C (2, 6), D (2, 5), E (5, 1), F (0, 0), G (3, 6), H (6, 3), I (6, 5), J (5, 0), K (1, 6), L (4, 0), with kNN lists of 8 ($d_{init} = 2d$) pruned to $d = 4$.

blocks.prompt: Node K at (1, 6) has 8 kNN neighbors in order C, D, G, B, I, H, A, F. F is the farthest (6.08). We keep d = 4 edges. Will the edge K to F survive?
blocks.reveal: Yes. F has only **1 detour** (only A lists F), while B, I, H have 3, 4 and 5 detours. The kept edges are C (0), D (1), G (2) and F (1). The farthest kNN neighbor survives because nothing else leads to it; this is the same effect as alpha above 1 in Vamana.

blocks.title: Detour matrix for node K (1 = Z ranks before Y and lists Y)

scenes.caption: Rows are K's neighbors Z, columns are targets Y, both in rank order. A 1 means the edge K to Y can be bypassed via Z. Column sums are the detour counts.
B, I, H have 3, 4, 5 detours: three to five closer neighbors already link to them. These edges are redundant.
F (rank 7, the farthest) has a single detour, via A. Few alternatives mean the edge is valuable, so it is kept despite its length.

blocks.title: Node K: from 8 kNN edges to 4 CAGRA edges

scenes.caption: The kNN list of K sorted by distance (computed from grid coordinates), with each edge's detour count.
Sort by (detours, rank) and keep d = 4: C (0), D (1), F (1), G (2). B, I, H, A are pruned.
Reverse edges: C, D and G keep K in their pruned lists, so K gets reverse candidates C, D, G. The merge takes d/2 = 2 from each side: C, D from the pruned list, then G, then F fills the last slot.

blocks.md: **Reverse edges.** After pruning, CAGRA builds the reversed graph: Y gets an edge back to X for each kept edge X to Y, ordered by that edge's rank in X's pruned list and capped at $d$. Then it merges: take $d/2$ neighbors from the pruned graph and $d/2$ from the reversed graph, filling from the pruned graph if there are too few reverse edges. In the toy graph, node F gains an edge to K this way, linking the bottom-left cluster to the top-left one.

The paper measures two properties. **Strongly connected components**: fewer is better, since a search may not escape a component. **Average 2-hop node count**: how many nodes are reachable in two steps, at most $d + d^2$: $d$ nodes one hop away, and each of them has $d$ neighbors of its own. Reordering raises the 2-hop count most; reverse edges cut the number of strong components most. Rank-based reordering was up to 1.9x faster than distance-based reordering, which ran out of memory on DEEP-100M (100 million 96-dimensional image descriptors from the Deep1B benchmark, computed by a deep neural network; Babenko and Lempitsky, CVPR 2016), with almost the same recall and throughput.

In the cuVS implementation the detour count is simply the number of closer neighbors whose kNN list contains Y; the paper describes the test with ranks of both hops (max of the two ranks below the edge's rank). Both use rank instead of distance.

blocks.question: Why does CAGRA use rank-based reordering instead of computing distances between neighbors?
options: Ranks give strictly better graphs
Distance-based reordering needs about N x d_init x (d_init - 1) distance computations or an N x d_init distance table, which is slow or runs out of memory at scale
GPUs cannot compute distances
NN-descent does not produce sorted lists
blocks.explain: The paper reports that distance-based reordering was slower and hit out-of-memory on DEEP-100M, while rank-based reordering gave almost the same recall-throughput curve. The rank is a free proxy because NN-descent already sorted each list by distance.

blocks.question: A CAGRA graph built with intermediate degree 128 and graph degree 64 gives too low recall even with large search settings. Per the cuVS tuning guide, what is the build-side knob to try after graph_degree?
options: Lower intermediate_graph_degree
Disable reverse edges
Increase intermediate_graph_degree, giving pruning more choices
Set alpha = 1.2
blocks.explain: cuVS suggests tuning itopk_size (the search-time list size, covered in the next lesson) first, then graph_degree, then intermediate_graph_degree if graph quality is still too low. A larger kNN graph gives the pruning step more candidates, at a higher build cost. CAGRA has no alpha parameter.

lessons.title: CAGRA search on the GPU, and picking an index

blocks.md: CAGRA search keeps one contiguous buffer per query: an **internal top-M list** (the best M nodes so far, $M \ge k$; cuVS calls it `itopk_size`) followed by a **candidate list** of $p \times d$ slots, where $p$ is the number of parents expanded per iteration (`search_width`, default 1) and $d$ the graph degree. Here $p$ counts parents; it is not the node $p$ of lesson 2, and $M$ is a list length, not HNSW's $M$. Each entry is a node id and its distance to the query.

One iteration has three steps:

1. **Top-M update**: keep the M smallest distances from the whole buffer (top list plus candidates).
2. **Graph traversal**: pick the best $p$ nodes in the top-M list that have not been parents yet, and copy all their neighbor ids into the candidate list.
3. **Distance calculation**: compute distances only for nodes seen for the first time; a visited-node hash table filters the rest.

The search stops when the top-M ids stop changing, and returns the first $k$.
Here it runs on the toy CAGRA graph from lesson 7 (12 points, $d = 4$), with $M = 4$, $p = 1$, query at (0, 6). Distances are Euclidean on the grid and were computed by script.

blocks.title: CAGRA search buffer, iteration by iteration

scenes.caption: Step 0: sample p x d = 4 random nodes (E, H, A, L) and compute their distances to the query at (0, 6). Step 1 copies the best M = 4 into the top-M list. Parent: A.
Step 2 copies parent A's 4 neighbors into the candidate list. Step 3 scores only first-time nodes: L was already scored, so it is skipped. B (4.24) jumps to the top. Next parent: B.
B's neighbors are D, E, A, F; only D is new (2.24). Three of four slots were wasted on known nodes, which the hash table detects cheaply. Next parent: D.
D's neighbors C, G, B, K bring three new nodes, including K at 1.00, the true nearest neighbor. Next parent: K.
K's neighbors C, D, G, F are all known, so the top-M list is unchanged: the search has converged. Return the top k entries, here K (1.00) and C (2.00).

blocks.md:
GPU details that make this fast, from the paper:

- **Warp splitting**: one distance is computed by a *team* of 4, 8, 16 or 32 threads (the cuVS `team_size`). A 96-d float vector is 3072 bits (96 x 32), less than the 4096 bits a full warp loads with 128-bit loads (32 threads x 128 bits), so one distance per warp would leave a quarter of the warp idle; teams of 8 let one warp compute four distances at once.
- **Sorting**: top-M merges use a warp-level bitonic sort (a sorting network: a fixed, data-independent pattern of compare-and-swap steps, so all 32 threads do the same work) when the candidate buffer has at most 512 entries, and a radix-based sort across the CTA above that.
- **Forgettable hash table**: in single-CTA mode the visited table lives in shared memory (typically 4 KB or less per query) and is periodically reset, keeping only the current top-M. Recomputing a few distances is cheaper than a big table.
- **Parent flag**: whether a node has been a parent is stored in the top bit of its id, which limits a 32-bit index to $2^{31} - 1$ nodes.

**Single-CTA vs multi-CTA.** Single-CTA maps one query to one thread block, good for large batches (100 and up). For small batches that would leave most of the GPU idle, multi-CTA runs one query on several CTAs that each expand one parent and share a hash table in device memory (the GPU's large main memory, slower than shared memory). The paper uses multi-CTA when the batch is smaller than the number of SMs or when M exceeds 512. In cuVS, `algo = AUTO` makes this choice.

blocks.title: CAGRA speedups reported in the paper (upper end of each range)

scenes.caption: Graph build: 2.2 to 27x faster than HNSW. Large-batch search at 90 to 95 percent recall: 33 to 77x HNSW and 3.8 to 8.8x other GPU methods.

Lower ends of the same ranges. Single-query search: 3.4 to 53x faster than HNSW at 95 percent recall, thanks to multi-CTA. Ranges depend on dataset and hardware (an NVIDIA A100 GPU versus a 64-core AMD EPYC CPU).

from cuvs.neighbors import cagra, hnsw

# build on the GPU (defaults: intermediate_graph_degree=128, graph_degree=64)
index = cagra.build(cagra.IndexParams(graph_degree=64), dataset)

# search on the GPU: itopk_size is the main recall knob (default 64)
distances, neighbors = cagra.search(
    cagra.SearchParams(itopk_size=128), index, queries, 10)

# or convert to HNSW and serve on CPUs
hnsw_index = hnsw.from_cagra(hnsw.IndexParams(hierarchy="gpu"), index)
blocks.caption: cuVS Python API as shown in the cuVS CAGRA guide; parameter defaults from its tables.

blocks.md: **CAGRA to HNSW.** cuVS can convert a CAGRA graph into an hnswlib-format HNSW index, so GPUs do the expensive build and CPUs serve queries. The `hierarchy` option chooses a base-layer-only index (`NONE`) or a full index with upper layers built on the CPU or GPU. The guide also advises not keeping the dataset attached to the CAGRA index when converting right after build (`attach_dataset_on_build = False` in C++).

Choosing: **DiskANN** when the data is far larger than RAM and an SSD is acceptable (a few ms per query at high recall on one machine). **CAGRA** when vectors fit in GPU memory and you need high throughput or fast builds; IVF-PQ initial graph builds can run in batches on datasets larger than GPU memory. **CAGRA then HNSW** when you build on GPUs but serve on CPUs.

**When the vectors do not fit in GPU memory.** The cuVS guide's baseline after build is the dataset, $N \times D \times B$ bytes ($B$ = 4 for fp32), plus the graph, $N \times G \times 4$ bytes with 32-bit ids and $G$ = graph_degree, and search needs both resident in GPU memory. For 100M 96-d float32 vectors at graph_degree 64 that is 38.4 GB + 25.6 GB = 64 GB before any workspace, more than many GPUs hold. The documented ways out: build the kNN graph with IVF-PQ in batches or with ACE partitions, attach a compressed dataset (the `compression` build parameter; with CAGRA-Q the original vectors can stay in host memory), or convert to HNSW and serve on CPUs, detaching the dataset after build.

blocks.question: In the toy search, the query's true nearest neighbor K was not in the random start sample. How did the search reach it?
options: The hash table stored K's distance in advance
Each iteration expanded the best non-parent node (A, then B, then D), and D's neighbor list contained K
Multi-CTA mode searched all nodes
K was added by the reverse-edge step during search
blocks.explain: Search moves through parents: A gave B, B gave D, and D's out-edges include K. The top-M list stopped changing after K was expanded, so the search ended. Reverse edges matter at build time, not search time.

blocks.question: A recommendation service sends one query at a time to a GPU CAGRA index, and the GPU is mostly idle. Which setting addresses this?
options: Multi-CTA search, which spreads one query across several thread blocks
A larger team_size
A smaller graph_degree
Single-CTA with a persistent kernel
blocks.explain: Single-CTA maps a query to one block, so a batch of 1 uses a sliver of the GPU. Multi-CTA assigns several CTAs to one query, each expanding a parent, which the paper designed for batch sizes of about 1 to 100. cuVS AUTO selects it for small batches.

lessons.title: Build and measure: DiskANN and CAGRA indexes end to end

blocks.md: Every knob in this course, $R$, $L$, $W$, the PQ bytes, `itopk_size`, trades recall against cost. A recall number without its cost means nothing, and so does a QPS number without its recall. This lesson walks the full loop: write the data, build, sweep a search knob, and read the curve. DiskANN's tools read a plain binary format, `.bin`: a 4-byte integer count $n$, a 4-byte integer dimension $d$, then the $n \times d$ values row by row. For SIFT10K that is $8 + 10000 \times 128 \times 4 = 5{,}120{,}008$ bytes.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np, os

def fvecs(path):
    a = np.fromfile(path, dtype="int32")
    return a.reshape(-1, a[0] + 1)[:, 1:].copy().view("float32")

def write_bin(path, x):
    n, d = x.shape
    with open(path, "wb") as f:
        np.array([n, d], dtype="int32").tofile(f)  # 4-byte count, 4-byte dim
        x.astype("float32").tofile(f)              # then n x d values, row by row

xb = fvecs("siftsmall/siftsmall_base.fvecs")
write_bin("siftsmall_base.bin", xb)
print(xb.shape, os.path.getsize("siftsmall_base.bin"))
print(np.fromfile("siftsmall_base.bin", dtype="int32", count=2))
# (10000, 128) 5120008
# [10000   128]
blocks.caption: Converting SIFT10K from the TEXMEX fvecs format to DiskANN's .bin format (run here; output shown). The repository also ships a fvecs_to_bin tool.

blocks.md:
**Building.** `build_disk_index` takes the knobs from lessons 2 to 4:

- `-R` max degree (default 64, typically 60 to 150) and `-L` build list size (default 100, typically 75 to 200, at least $R$).
- `-B` search RAM budget in GB, which sets the PQ code size; the docs' 100K-point example passes 0.003 GB, which implies 32-byte codes ($100000 \times 32$ bytes is 0.003 GB).
- `-M` build RAM budget; below a one-shot build's needs it switches to the overlapping divide-and-conquer build.
- `--PQ_disk_bytes` 0 (the default) keeps full vectors on the SSD, so recall can approach 100 percent.

blocks.code:
# from the repository's SSD index docs: 100K SIFT points, R = 32, L = 50
./apps/utils/compute_groundtruth --data_type float --dist_fn l2 \
    --base_file data/sift/sift_learn.fbin --query_file data/sift/sift_query.fbin \
    --gt_file data/sift/sift_query_learn_gt100 --K 100
./apps/build_disk_index --data_type float --dist_fn l2 \
    --data_path data/sift/sift_learn.fbin \
    --index_path_prefix data/sift/disk_index_sift_learn_R32_L50_A1.2 \
    -R 32 -L50 -B 0.003 -M 1
./apps/search_disk_index --data_type float --dist_fn l2 \
    --index_path_prefix data/sift/disk_index_sift_learn_R32_L50_A1.2 \
    --query_file data/sift/sift_query.fbin --gt_file data/sift/sift_query_learn_gt100 \
    -K 10 -L 10 20 30 40 50 100 --result_path data/sift/res --num_nodes_to_cache 10000

blocks.md: **Searching and reading the output.** `search_disk_index` sweeps a list of `-L` values (each at least $K$) at a beam width `-W` (default 2), with `--num_nodes_to_cache` nodes held in RAM and `-T` threads, one query per thread. For each L it prints QPS, mean and 99.9th-percentile latency in microseconds, mean 4 KB reads, CPU time and recall@10. More threads raise QPS but share the SSD's IOPS, so per-query latency can rise. The plot below takes the docs' own run (the one from lesson 3) and turns it into a curve.

blocks.title: Recall@10 versus QPS: the docs' DiskANN run, 100K SIFT, W = 2

scenes.caption: Each point is one L. Moving left trades QPS for recall: 27,724 QPS at 81.8 percent (L = 10), 3,338 QPS at 99.9 percent (L = 100).
Target 95 percent: the fastest point above the line is L = 20, 15,369 QPS and 15.9 reads per query. L = 30 would cost a third of the throughput for 2.4 more points.
Target 99 percent: now L = 40 (7,684 QPS, 30.8 reads) is the cheapest point above the line. Each extra nine of recall roughly halves throughput here.

blocks.md: **How to measure honestly.** Measure recall@10 against exact ground truth on held-out queries. Report QPS at a stated thread count together with mean and tail latency (p99 or p99.9), and for SSD indexes the mean reads and round trips per query, which predict behavior on other hardware better than wall time. Sweep the search knob ($L$ for DiskANN, `itopk_size` for CAGRA) and compare whole curves, or compare at one fixed recall. The NeurIPS 2023 Big-ANN competition ranks its filtered, out-of-distribution and sparse tracks exactly this way: QPS at 90 percent recall@10.

We cannot run the C++ tools here, so the bars below come from lesson 3's simulator on SIFT10K (our Vamana graph, 32-byte PQ steering, no node cache). The shape matches the docs' run: reads grow almost linearly with $L$ while recall saturates. The docs read fewer nodes at small $L$ (8.8 at $L = 10$ against our 17.3) likely in part because they cache 10,000 nodes near the start, which removes the first hops' reads, and they search a different, 100K-point graph.

blocks.title: Sweeping L on SIFT10K (our simulator, 100 queries)

scenes.caption: Reads per query at W = 2: 17.3, 26.6, 36.1, 45.8, 55.6, 104.9, close to L plus a constant.
Round trips per query at W = 2: 9.4, 14.1, 18.8, 23.6, 28.6, 53.1, about half the reads.
Round trips at W = 4: 7.0, 9.0, 11.5, 13.5, 16.2, 28.2. From L = 20 up, recall matches W = 2 to within 0.1 points, while reads rise by 3.6 to 4.8 per query.

blocks.question: From the simulator's W = 2 sweep, you need at least 95 percent recall@10 with the fewest SSD reads. Which L do you pick?
options: L = 10: 84.5 percent with 17.3 reads
L = 40: 99.8 percent with 45.8 reads
L = 20: 97.7 percent with 26.6 reads
L = 100, to be safe
blocks.explain: L = 20 is the smallest L above the target. L = 10 misses it; L = 40 and L = 100 pay 1.7x and 3.9x the reads for recall you did not ask for. In production, re-check the choice on real queries, since the target is a mean over queries.

blocks.md: **CAGRA with cuVS.** The Python API mirrors lessons 7 and 8. `cagra.IndexParams` takes `graph_degree` (default 64), `intermediate_graph_degree` (default 128) and `build_algo`; `cagra.SearchParams` takes `itopk_size` (default 64, at least $k$, the main knob) and `search_width` (default 1). Sweep `itopk_size` to trace the recall-QPS curve, just as you swept $L$. Filtered search takes a bitset, one bit per vector, 1 meaning allowed. cuVS estimates the filtered fraction $f$ from the bitset and, in the current source's multi-CTA planner, raises `itopk_size` to $k/(1-f) + (\text{itopk} - k)/\sqrt{1-f}$, rounded up to a multiple of 32: for $k = 10$, itopk 64 and $f = 0.99$ that is 1,568. The guide warns that results are not guaranteed to match exact filtered search, especially for highly selective filters without an accurate filtering rate.

blocks.code:
import cupy as cp, numpy as np
from cuvs.neighbors import cagra, filters, hnsw

index = cagra.build(cagra.IndexParams(intermediate_graph_degree=128,
                                      graph_degree=64, build_algo="nn_descent"),
                    cp.asarray(xb))
for itopk in (16, 32, 64, 128, 256):   # trace the recall-QPS curve
    sp = cagra.SearchParams(itopk_size=itopk, search_width=1)
    distances, neighbors = cagra.search(sp, index, cp.asarray(xq), 10)
    # time this call over many batches; compare neighbors with exact ground truth

bits = np.zeros((len(xb) + 31) // 32, dtype=np.uint32)
for i in allowed_ids:                   # bit 1 = allowed
    bits[i // 32] |= np.uint32(1 << (i % 32))
distances, neighbors = cagra.search(cagra.SearchParams(), index, cp.asarray(xq), 10,
                                    filter=filters.from_bitset(cp.asarray(bits)))

cpu_index = hnsw.from_cagra(hnsw.IndexParams(hierarchy="gpu"), index)
blocks.caption: Not run here: needs an NVIDIA GPU and the cuvs package. Names and defaults follow the cuVS CAGRA guide and the Python bindings (cagra.pyx); xb, xq and allowed_ids stand for your data.

blocks.md: One recipe for both indexes: fix the data and exact ground truth, build once, sweep one search knob, and plot recall against QPS (plus reads and round trips on SSD). Choose the cheapest point above your recall target, then confirm its tail latency at your real thread count or batch size.

blocks.question: A CAGRA service filters each query to one tenant's vectors, 0.5 percent of the index, and returns fewer correct neighbors than exact filtered search. What should you check first?
options: Whether the filter's filtering rate reaches the planner (or itopk_size is raised by hand), since a highly selective filter needs a much longer internal list
Lower graph_degree to save memory
Switch the metric to inner product
Use team_size 32
blocks.explain: With 99.5 percent of nodes filtered out, almost every entry in a 64-slot internal list is invalid. cuVS's multi-CTA planner raises itopk_size from the filtering rate when it knows it (single-CTA does not, so raise it by hand there), and its guide warns that selective filters without an accurate rate can miss neighbors. Degree, metric and team size do not address the list running out of valid entries.
